syllabus.clause: async fn in traits and return-position impl Trait in traits have been stable since 1.75. The "Send bound problem": callers cannot require the returned future to be Send. Return-type notation (RFC 3654) would fix it but is still unstable in 2026. Workarounds: trait-variant, the boxing async-trait, and dynosaur for dyn dispatch.

items.item: A trait containing an async fn is not dyn compatible: building a vtable requires every method's return type to be known and uniform across implementors, but an async fn's return type is an anonymous, per-implementor-sized future, so the compiler refuses outright with error E0038 rather than guessing at a layout.

at.step: No — the compiler's own diagnostic says exactly why

items.item: The Send bound problem is not about whether a specific implementor's future happens to be Send — it is that the trait definition itself gives callers no syntax to require it, so even a fully generic, Send-bounded implementor cannot satisfy a generic caller that needs the returned future to be Send.

at.step: rustc's own diagnostic: the trait's future cannot be sent between threads

items.item: trait-variant's fix is deliberately not a modification of the original trait: it generates an entirely separate, additional trait with the desired bound, and implementors choose which one (or both) to implement, so existing single-threaded users of the original trait are never forced to adopt the bound.

at.step: trait_variant::make fixes this by generating a second, Send-bounded trait

items.item: Fixing the Send bound problem does nothing for dyn compatibility, and fixing dyn compatibility does nothing for the Send bound problem — they are two independent gaps in today's stable language, caused by two different limitations (vtable construction versus bound expressiveness), and each needs its own workaround.

at.step: Does fixing Send also fix dyn dispatch?

items.item: async-trait's fix is type erasure: every async method is rewritten to return Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send>>, a single concrete, dyn-compatible type regardless of which implementor produced it, which is exactly what makes dyn dispatch possible again.

at.step: async-trait fixes dyn dispatch instead — by boxing every call

items.item: That type erasure is not free: producing a Pin<Box<dyn Future>> requires one real heap allocation per call, measured directly here with a counting global allocator rather than merely cited from the macro's documentation — a cost real production code accepts deliberately in exchange for dyn dispatch, not an accident.

at.step: Measured, not assumed: one real heap allocation, every call

items.item: Return-Type Notation (RFC 3654) is named as the eventual native fix for the Send bound problem specifically — letting a caller write a bound like G::greet(): Send directly — but it remains unstable as of 2026, so trait-variant's generated-sibling-trait approach is the practical answer today, not a stopgap nobody expects to last.

at.step: Recap: two gaps, two separate fixes, proven both ways

items.item: dynosaur is named as a further, more recent workaround specifically for dyn-safe async traits, built on different internal machinery than async-trait's boxing approach; this topic does not build an executable example of it, consistent with naming a real tool without asserting specifics this topic did not verify by running it.

at.step: Recap: two gaps, two separate fixes, proven both ways

items.item: In production, the choice between trait-variant and async-trait is a real design decision: trait-variant costs nothing at the call site (it is just a second trait) but requires generic code, while async-trait enables dyn dispatch and heterogeneous collections at the cost of one allocation per call — exactly the kind of tradeoff the advertising-platform example from async-trait's own documentation is built to motivate.

at.step: async-trait fixes dyn dispatch instead — by boxing every call

items.item: This topic closes Chapter 8 on a deliberately honest note: not every gap in async Rust has a native, stable fix as of 2026, and naming a real, currently-unsolved limitation precisely (rather than glossing over it) is exactly what distinguishes production-grade understanding from a tutorial that only shows the happy path.

at.step: Recap: two gaps, two separate fixes, proven both ways
